w: Fifty-one slender cast-iron figures, each abstracted from a laser scan of a Menzies resident, stand scattered across ten square kilometres of a dry outback salt lake. Installed for the 2003 Perth Festival and never removed, it has become one of the largest permanent outdoor sculpture installations on earth.
s: 51 iron figures scattered across a dry salt lake
_facts: Antony Gormley's largest permanent outdoor work, in remote outback WA

w: A private working farm on the Kaipara Harbour doubles as a sculpture park holding outdoor pieces by Richard Serra, Anish Kapoor, Andy Goldsworthy and Neil Dawson, scattered across rolling paddocks grazed by exotic livestock. Entry is free, but the farm opens to the public only a handful of days each year.
s: Monumental sculpture on a working farm by the harbour
_facts: One of the world's largest private outdoor sculpture collections

w: Fifty years and roughly 40 million dollars in the making, Michael Heizer's mile-and-a-half-long earthwork of sculpted concrete mounds, ramps and mesas rises from a remote high-desert valley. Completed in 2022, it admits only six visitors a day by reservation, making it one of the hardest artworks on earth to see.
s: A mile-long earthwork, 50 years in the making
_facts: The largest contemporary sculpture ever built, finished after half a century

w: Belgian sculptor Albert Szukalski's ghostly plaster-shrouded Last Supper figures stand in open desert beside the abandoned mining town of Rhyolite, joined since 1984 by a pink cinderblock couch, a mosaic sofa girl and other outdoor sculptures. Free and unstaffed, it sits at the edge of Death Valley.
s: Ghost-town sculpture garden on the Death Valley edge
_facts: Free, always-open outdoor sculpture museum beside a genuine ghost town

w: Ninety hectares of parkland in China's industrial northeast hold more than 340 sculptures by artists from over 130 countries, gathered through international symposia since the park opened in 2003. Surrealist bronzes and stone monoliths sit half-hidden among trees, forming a vast open-air collection.
s: 340-plus sculptures from 130 countries in one park
_facts: One of the world's largest international outdoor sculpture collections

w: A 100-metre steel cube clad in nearly 10,000 square metres of mirror sits in a desert canyon near AlUla, reflecting the sandstone cliffs and sky until its walls seem to dissolve into the landscape. Opened in 2019 and holding a Guinness record as the largest mirrored building on earth, it also serves as a concert hall.
s: The world's largest mirrored building, in a desert canyon
_facts: A record-holding mirrored landmark anchoring Saudi Arabia's new art valley

w: A French New Wave-styled cocktail room on Rruga Pjeter Bogdani, Nouvelle Vague debuted at No. 28 on the World's 50 Best Bars 2025, the first Albanian bar ever ranked. Black-and-white film stills and jazz set the mood for a menu leaning on Balkan produce and vintage aperitif technique.
s: Albania's first-ever World's 50 Best bar
_facts: First Albanian entry on World's 50 Best Bars, debuted No.28 in 2025

w: Tucked behind a nondescript Cantonese grocery shopfront in old Dongshankou, Hope & Sesame turns Lingnan ingredients, congee, herbal tonics, five-spice, into serious cocktails. A decade in, it became Guangzhou's first World's 50 Best entry in 2025, landing at No. 29 globally and No. 7 in Asia.
s: Cantonese cocktails behind a grocery-shop facade
_facts: Guangzhou's first-ever World's 50 Best Bars entry, No.29 in 2025

w: A no-frills tasting room on Route 1 outside Portland pours the beers that built Maine Beer Company's cult reputation, Lunch IPA and Dinner double IPA chief among them, brewed by a company giving a slice of every sale to charity. Bottles rarely leave New England, so the pilgrimage is the only way to drink it fresh.
s: Cult IPA brewery, Lunch and Dinner pilgrimage site
_facts: One of New England's most cult-followed craft breweries; Lunch and Dinner IPAs are benchmark beers

w: Thatched-roof ryokan founded in the Edo era, oldest of seven inns scattered through Nyuto Onsenkyo's beech forest. Four distinct springs feed its wooden tubs, from milky shirayu to dark kuroyu, pooling in a mixed-gender outdoor bath that steams above the snow. Feudal lords once came here to take the cure.
s: Edo-era ryokan with milky mountain baths
_facts: Widely ranked Japan's most atmospheric onsen retreat

w: Three-storey wooden bathhouse built in 1894 over a spring cited in eighth-century chronicles as one of Japan's oldest, once visited by emperors and princes. Its turreted facade, tiled soaking rooms and a mikoyu chamber reserved for imperial guests reputedly inspired the bathhouse in Spirited Away.
s: Japan's storied 1894 bathhouse, oldest spring
_facts: National Important Cultural Property, among Japan's oldest onsen

w: Steam rises over Yubatake, the wooden-troughed 'hot water field' at the town centre where scalding sulfuric spring water is channelled and cooled before reaching the bathhouses. Kusatsu has topped Japan's onsen-town rankings for decades; bathers still perform yumomi, paddling the water with long boards by hand.
s: Japan's perennial top-ranked onsen town
_facts: Repeatedly voted Japan's number-one hot spring resort

w: Eight scalding geothermal pools, too hot to bathe in, are toured instead as a spectacle: cobalt-blue Umi Jigoku, blood-red Chinoike Jigoku, and a crater of grey mud that plops and belches. Beppu itself pumps out more hot-spring water than anywhere else on earth, feeding thousands of onsen across the city.
s: Boiling 'hell' pools, too hot to enter
_facts: Japan's most extreme geothermal spectacle, highest onsen output

w: A trail through Steam Valley climbs past hissing fumaroles and bubbling mudpots to Klambragil, a river warmed by geothermal runoff to soaking temperature. Wooden platforms and a duckboard path let bathers wade in and drift downstream; unlike Iceland's built lagoons, entry is free and the water is entirely wild.
s: Free wild river, warm enough to swim in
_facts: Iceland's best-known free hike-in hot river bathing spot

a: Los Rios Region, Villarrica National Park
w: Twenty slate-lined pools step down a forested ravine, linked by a red-stained wooden footbridge heated from beneath by the thermal channel it follows. Architect German del Sol carved the complex from more than 60 natural springs emerging at 80C, cooled to a soakable 45C amid ferns and native coigue trees.
s: 20 slate pools threaded through a ravine
_facts: Landmark of thermal-spa architecture, widely called Chile's best

w: Reachable only by boat across the Ventisquero fjord, stone pools sit at the waterline where hot spring runoff meets the tide, framed by rainforest and glacier-topped peaks. The water carries magnesium, chromium and zinc from source temperatures near 80C, tempered to around 40C by the time it reaches the pools.
s: Fjord-side pools reached only by boat
_facts: Patagonia's most remote and scenic thermal bathing spot

a: Guanacaste, near Rincon de la Vieja
w: Fed by eight springs along a volcanic gorge near Miravalles, a mile of naturally hot river runs cool at one end and near-scalding at the other, letting bathers pick their own temperature among rock pools. Stone stairways descend into the deep canyon, with volcanic mud banks free for a self-applied facial.
s: A mile of self-mixing volcanic hot river
_facts: Rare thermal river you can walk and choose your own temperature

w: A milky-blue thermal river cuts through a desert canyon in the Sierra Madre foothills, spilling from a steaming cave you can wade shoulder-deep into past hanging bats. Terraced infinity pools cling to the cliffside above, fed by more than 30 hot springs at roughly 35C, with a suspension bridge crossing the gorge.
s: Milky-blue river pouring from a hot cave
_facts: One of Mexico's most visually striking natural hot spring canyons

w: Springs emerging at up to 80C beside the Parvati River cook communal langar meals for pilgrims at the adjoining Sikh gurdwara and Hindu Ram temple, both tied to a Puranic legend of Shiva and Parvati's lost earring. Bathhouses along the riverbank offer the scalding water free to travellers and sadhus alike.
s: Sacred spring that cooks pilgrims' meals
_facts: Himalayan pilgrimage hot spring shared by Hindus and Sikhs since the 15th century

w: Wood-fired since 1906, this stone-walled public sauna in the working-class Pispala district is the oldest in Finland still operating on its original site. Meter-long logs feed a stove weighing over a tonne beneath separate men's and women's rooms; regulars have queued here for a whisk-and-steam session for generations.
s: Finland's oldest wood-fired public sauna
_facts: Continuously operating since 1906, a living piece of sauna culture

w: Founded in 1808 by actor-turned-entrepreneur Sila Sandunov and rebuilt in palatial style in 1896, Moscow's grandest banya pairs Baroque stucco halls with wood-fired steam rooms and plunge pools once fed by a private aqueduct. Pushkin, Tolstoy and Chekhov all passed through its marble corridors on the way to the whisk.
s: 1896 marble banya loved by Tolstoy, Pushkin
_facts: Russia's most opulent historic bathhouse, still in daily use

w: Instead of a piazza, this Val d'Orcia hamlet centres on a medieval pool of 52C spring water, built over the Roman source that drew Lorenzo the Magnificent and Saint Catherine of Siena seeking cures. Swimming in the square pool is forbidden now, but the water runs free into rock pools at the Park of the Mills below.
s: A whole village square filled with hot water
_facts: Italy's only town whose main square is a thermal pool

w: Terraced geothermal pools of varying temperature climb a hillside above Fingal, tapping bore water drawn from 637 metres underground and cooled through a cascade of cave pools, a hilltop bath with 360-degree views, and a reflexology walk. Opened in 2005, it anchors Australia's largest natural hot-springs culture.
s: Terraced bore-water pools above Port Phillip
_facts: Australia's largest and best-known natural hot springs complex

w: Six sulfur springs rise through tectonic cracks in a limestone canyon and pool in shallow stone baths beside the arched Ottoman-era Kadiu bridge, the water settling around a mild 22-28C. Long used by shepherds for skin and joint complaints, the springs sit inside a canyon reached only by a rough gravel track.
s: Sulfur pools by an Ottoman stone bridge
_facts: Albania's best-known wild thermal baths, largely untouched by development

w: A fenced jet of mineral water erupts several metres into the air at a scalding 103C, the only active geyser on the Balkan Peninsula and among Europe's hottest springs. It sits at the edge of a small spa town otherwise built around milder pools, with Rila Monastery within easy reach.
s: The Balkans' only true erupting geyser
_facts: Hottest spring in Europe, the Balkans' sole active geyser

w: A bush-lined stream near the Wai-O-Tapu geothermal field cascades over shallow rock ledges into naturally warmed pools shaded by native forest, entirely free save for a car park and a short track down to the water. Named for the diesel-like sulfur smell that lingers, it is one of the last wild soaks left near Rotorua.
s: Free forest stream warmed by volcanic heat
_facts: Rotorua's best-loved free, undeveloped hot spring soak

w: Twice a day, for about two hours either side of low tide, geothermal water rises through the sand of an ordinary Pacific beach hot enough to dig your own spa pool with a hired spade. Two hot springs beneath the sand can reach 64C, cooled by mixing in seawater as the tide pulls back along the Coromandel coast.
s: Dig your own hot pool in the sand
_facts: A whole beach that becomes a DIY hot spring at low tide

w: A hike through old-growth Douglas fir leads to hand-hewn cedar tubs fed by wooden flumes from a spring first used by Native peoples and named for an 1880 prospector, Bob Bagby. Volunteers rebuilt the bathhouses after a 1979 fire, and the open-air soak remains a Pacific Northwest backcountry rite of passage.
s: Cedar tubs, a forest hike from the road
_facts: Oregon's classic backcountry hot spring, rebuilt by volunteers since 1981

w: An 8.5-mile trail gaining 2,500 feet ends above treeline at 11,200 feet, where mineral water surfacing at 122F pools into soaking spots ringed by 14,000-foot peaks of the Maroon Bells wilderness. A permit system now caps overnight numbers, but it remains one of the highest, most dramatic hot springs in the Rockies.
s: Alpine soak at 11,200ft below 14ers
_facts: One of the highest-altitude, most scenic backcountry hot springs in the US

w: Discovered by gold-mining brothers in 1905 and now powered by its own geothermal heat, this remote resort 60 miles from Fairbanks pairs a mineral-rich outdoor rock lake with some of the darkest, clearest skies for aurora viewing in North America. An ice museum carved year-round from chilled ice sits beside the springs.
s: Geothermal lake under the northern lights
_facts: Alaska's premier hot spring, run on its own geothermal power

w: Regarded as sacred by Tewa peoples for over a thousand years before an 1868 bathhouse made it one of America's first health resorts, this high-desert spring is unique for four distinct mineral waters -- arsenic, iron, soda and lithium -- with no sulfur smell. The 1916 hotel remains on the National Register.
s: Four unique mineral waters, no sulfur smell
q: Ojo Caliente Mineral Springs Ojo Caliente
_facts: One of America's oldest health resorts, sacred to the Tewa for centuries

w: A sulfurous spring trickles down a low waterfall into shallow stone basins beside the ancient fortress ruins of Nokalakevi, an early capital of the Georgian kingdom of Egrisi. Unmarked and unheated by any resort, the pale mineral pools sit in open countryside, still used informally by locals for skin ailments.
s: Wild sulfur falls by an ancient hillfort
_facts: An untouched wild spring beside one of Georgia's oldest fortress sites

w: Tucked into the San Benito district, this sensory coffee lab was founded by barista coach Federico Bolanos to showcase Salvadoran microlots through precise brewing and tasting flights. It placed third on the World's 100 Best Coffee Shops 2026 list, the highest ranking Central America has reached.
s: Salvadoran coffee lab ranked No.3 in the world
_facts: Ranked #3 worldwide in 2026, highest ever for Central America

w: Set on Pushkin Street, this was Yerevan's first dedicated specialty roastery, part of the Collective Group that helped seed the city's third-wave scene. State-of-the-art brewing gear and rotating single origins draw a growing crowd of Armenian coffee drinkers still discovering life beyond instant.
s: Armenia's first specialty coffee roastery
_facts: First specialty roastery in Armenia, still a scene anchor

w: Co-founded by six-time Canadian Barista Champion Ben Put, this Britannia flagship houses Monogram's roastery, training center and cafe. Precision espresso and rotating microlots have made it Calgary's most decorated specialty coffee name and a rising force in Canadian coffee competitions.
s: Flagship roastery of a six-time barista champion
_facts: Founder is a six-time Canadian Barista Champion

w: The Rogers flagship on East Walnut Avenue anchors Onyx's eight Northwest Arkansas locations, combining a full production roastery, barista training facility, bakery and cocktail bar. In 2026 it became the first American cafe ever named the World's Best Coffee Shop.
s: Named the world's best coffee shop in 2026
_facts: First-ever American winner of World's Best Coffee Shop, 2026

w: Eccentric English poet Edward James spent three decades and his fortune building over 30 concrete follies through a subtropical waterfall gorge: spiral stairs that end in midair, doorways framing nothing, a house that will in fact have five or six floors, all half-swallowed by jungle.
s: Surrealist concrete ruins swallowed by jungle
_facts: One of the world's great surrealist gardens, built alone by an eccentric heir deep in the Sierra Gorda rainforest

w: Duke Vicino Orsini carved a woodland of giant volcanic-stone monsters in the 1550s: a screaming ogre mouth big enough to picnic inside, a leaning house, an elephant crushing a soldier. Meant to unsettle rather than delight, it predates every later fashion for landscaped gardens.
s: 16th-century garden of giant stone monsters
q: Sacro Bosco (Park of the Monsters) Bomarzo
_facts: Considered the oldest sculpture garden of the modern era, built to disturb rather than please

w: Niki de Saint Phalle spent two decades raising 22 mirror- and mosaic-clad giants, one for each major arcana card. Visitors climb inside a voluptuous Empress sheathed in glass tile -- the artist's home during construction -- and wander among towers, sphinxes and a maze of reflective monsters.
s: Walk-in mosaic giants, one per tarot card
_facts: A monumental outsider-art garden you physically climb inside

w: A reclusive paper-mill worker spent fifty years alone carving nearly 500 concrete figures in his parents' garden: yoga-posed athletes, soldiers, animals, self-portraits, many fitted with real human teeth. He never explained the work and died in 2010; the park remains exactly as he left it.
s: 500 self-taught concrete figures in a pine forest
_facts: An entire outsider-art garden built alone by one obsessive rural sculptor over half a century

w: A retired physician and a sculptor turned their working dairy farm into 30 acres of garden rooms filled with kinetic scrap-metal creatures, a repurposed grain silo, ponds and allees, opened to the public as a nonprofit only in 2016 after decades as a private passion project.
s: Kinetic scrap-metal sculptures on an old dairy farm
_facts: Quietly one of New England's most inventive gardens, still little known outside regional circles

w: Artist Cesar Manrique carved a terraced amphitheater out of a disused quarry and lava tube, planting thousands of cacti from five continents around a restored 19th-century windmill. A giant articulated metal cactus sculpture, visible for miles, marks the entrance off the coastal road.
s: A cactus garden carved into a collapsed lava tube
_facts: Landscape art fusing raw volcanic terrain with a serious desert-plant collection

w: Wrapped around a bend of the Luosuo River since 1959, this is the largest outdoor tropical plant collection on earth: over 13,000 species across 38 themed zones, including giant Victoria water lilies that open at dusk and a clock flower that blooms on an almost hourly schedule.
s: 13,000 tropical species around a river bend
_facts: The world's most complete outdoor tropical botanical collection, still off most itineraries

w: Eighteen fully enclosed garden rooms recreate 4,000 years of garden history with no fences or plant labels breaking the illusion -- a Maori kitchen garden, an Italian Renaissance courtyard, a Ming Chinese scholar's garden, and a deliberately playful Surrealist Garden of oversized furniture.
s: Garden rooms spanning 4,000 years of design
_facts: A theatrical garden-of-gardens approach almost no other institution attempts

w: Founded in 1929 on the eastern edge of the capital, Central Asia's oldest botanical garden acclimatizes subtropical and Mediterranean species against a harsh, arid continental climate -- a rare stretch of unregimented green space inside one of the world's most closed and least-visited capitals.
s: Central Asia's oldest garden, in a closed capital
_facts: A century-old botanical institution inside one of the world's least-visited capital cities

w: Elsie Reford began transforming her salmon-fishing camp into a garden in 1926, eventually raising the northernmost great garden in eastern North America, famous for its blue Himalayan poppies. Since 2000 it has also hosted an annual International Garden Festival of experimental installations.
s: The northernmost great garden in eastern North America
_facts: A subarctic-latitude heritage garden plus an annual avant-garde design festival

w: Established in 1966 in a forested tribal district, Gujarat's largest botanical garden lays out separate plots recreating the state's arid, moist-deciduous, bamboo and scrub-forest habitats side by side, along with cactus, orchid and medicinal-plant collections along seven kilometres of paths.
s: A biodiversity park recreating Gujarat's forest types
_facts: An obscure state garden preserving forest habitats most visitors to India never encounter

w: Sixty hectares of sub-Andean forest above Ibague hold major orchid, bromeliad and palm collections and double as an active research station -- several new Anthurium and Xanthosoma species have been formally described here and published in international botanical journals.
s: A forest garden that keeps discovering new plants
_facts: An active taxonomic research garden still finding species new to science

w: At the foot of the Hex River Mountains, greenhouses and outdoor beds hold nearly 3,000 succulent species from around the world, set against roughly 400 species that grow wild in the surrounding Karoo semi-desert -- one of the planet's richest concentrations of succulent diversity.
s: Nearly 3,000 succulent species at the Karoo's edge
q: Karoo Desert National Botanical Garden Worcester
_facts: Arguably the single best place on Earth to see succulent plant diversity in one visit

w: Five hundred acres built almost entirely for tourism turn out to be scientifically serious: a dedicated Cycad Gene Bank holds more than 280 species, alongside orchid nurseries, a stone garden of imported boulders and avenues of elaborately clipped topiary shaped into animals and pagodas.
s: 500 acres and one of the world's largest cycad banks
_facts: An outsized private tourist garden with a genuinely important cycad conservation collection

w: Carmelite monks began planting exotic trees here in 1628 behind walls meant to keep the outside world out. A 1643 papal bull threatened excommunication for anyone who damaged a tree; Mexican cypress, Australian bunya pines and Californian redwoods now shade a fairy-tale neo-Manueline palace hotel.
s: A walled 17th-century forest guarded by papal decree
q: Bucaco Forest (Mata Nacional do Bucaco) Luso
_facts: One of Europe's oldest protected arboretums, historically enforced by threat of excommunication

w: Intha farmers weave long strips of water hyacinth and lake-bottom mud into buoyant beds anchored with bamboo poles, then pole between the rows by canoe to tend tomatoes and flowers. Some floating plots have been worked by the same families for generations, forming entire farming villages that ride the water.
s: Tomato farms rooted to woven mats that float
q: Inle Lake Floating Gardens Inle Lake
_facts: An entire agricultural landscape that literally floats on the surface of the lake

w: Diamond fever built an Edwardian town of 300 Germans in the Namib within a decade of a railway worker spotting a stone glinting in the sand in 1908. Richer fields further south drained it dry by the 1930s; abandoned by 1956, dunes have since poured through doors and windows, burying ballroom and bowling alley alike.
s: Diamond boomtown swallowed whole by desert sand
_facts: One of the world's most complete sand-reclaimed ghost towns

w: Sodium nitrate scraped from the driest desert on earth built an English-style town of nearly 4,000 workers, with a theatre, market and a pool cast from a ship's hull. Synthetic fertiliser and the Depression killed the trade; works closed in 1960 and stand untouched, a UNESCO-listed ghost town.
s: Nitrate boomtown left whole in the Atacama
_facts: Best-preserved nitrate mining ghost town on earth

w: Built in total secrecy under the codename Objekt 0774, this 3,000-square-metre, five-level bunker was Enver Hoxha's shelter against invasion and nuclear war, one of over 170,000 bunkers built across paranoid Communist Albania. Opened in 2014, its hundred concrete rooms now hold Cold War relics and art.
s: Dictator's five-storey doomsday bunker turned museum
_facts: The dictator's own nuclear-proof escape hatch, now public

w: Once the largest sulphur mine in Japan, this high-plateau complex housed over 15,000 workers in concrete blocks with then-luxurious central heating and flush toilets. Cheap refinery sulphur and falling demand bankrupted it by 1972. Acid drainage still bleeds pH-2 water, and fog often swallows the ruins whole.
s: Sulphur ghost town wrapped in permanent mist
_facts: Nicknamed Japan's real-life Silent Hill for its permanent mist

w: A future US president managed this Outback gold mine as a 23-year-old engineer in 1898, and the timber miners' cottages he oversaw still lean against the red dirt. Underground mining pulled 2.6 million ounces of gold before the shaft closed in 1963, emptying the town overnight and leaving it frozen mid-use.
s: Gold camp a young Herbert Hoover once ran
_facts: Ghost town once run by a future US president, Herbert Hoover

w: Gold fever drew thousands of prospectors to this bushveld camp in the 1890s, but a richer reef found on the Witwatersrand and rampant malaria emptied it almost as fast as it filled. Named for a Boer state secretary, it now counts a handful of residents among crumbling facades and one surviving colonial hotel.
s: Malarial gold-rush town abandoned within a decade
_facts: Boomed and emptied within a decade of South Africa's gold rush

w: Balti stonemasons raised this fortress-palace in the 16th century for a prince who fled Baltistan after a failed assassination, its timber halls said to have held a wind-powered rotating chamber famed as far as Lhasa. Dogra conquerors dismantled it in the 19th century, leaving a shell above the village.
s: Ladakhi fortress with a legendary spinning room
_facts: Remote Himalayan fort said to have had a rotating room

w: Moscow-subsidised lead ore mining built this settlement deep in the Karatau mountains, its ore trucked 150 kilometres to a Shymkent smelter. Independence killed the subsidies; the mine closed and the town all but emptied, leaving stone barrack rows, a school and a still-tended mosque scattered across the arid hillside.
s: Soviet lead-mining town left to the Karatau wind
_facts: Soviet mining town emptied almost overnight after 1991

w: Radon-rich springs made this the USSR's premier spa, drawing 125,000 visitors a year to 22 grand sanatoriums built partly by German POWs in Stalinist-classical marble. Soviet collapse and the 1992 Abkhaz war left displaced families living in the crumbling colonnades, which still stand half palace, half refuge.
s: Stalin-era marble spa town, now half refugee shelter
_facts: Soviet spa palaces now doubling as refugee housing

w: Founded as a mining camp in 1578, this Andean city has been consumed from inside for a century by the Raul Rojas open pit, one of the largest urban mines on earth. Whole neighbourhoods like Ayapoto were relocated as the crater crept outward; guided viewpoints now overlook streets ending abruptly at the pit's edge.
s: Viewpoint over a city being eaten by its own mine
q: Ayapoto (Cerro de Pasco open pit) Cerro de Pasco
_facts: A 400-year-old city literally being swallowed by its mine

w: Moorish, then Portuguese, defenders held this hilltop above the Guadiana from the 10th century on, its star-shaped bastions among the grandest on the Alentejo frontier. A gunpowder magazine blast in 1911 gutted the fortress and church; ivy-choked ramparts and a roofless nave now overlook Spain.
s: Star-fort ruin staring across the Spanish border
_facts: Star-fort blown apart by its own gunpowder store in 1911

w: Chrysotile asbestos pulled from this pit built, then slowly consumed, the town once literally named Asbestos, its crater growing two kilometres wide and 370 metres deep as streets were moved to make way for it. Mining stopped in 2011; a lookout platform, ringed by asbestos-flecked rockery, now overlooks the void.
s: Two-kilometre asbestos pit swallowing its own town
_facts: A town renamed itself to escape the stigma of its own pit

w: Silver, gold and mercury mines around this borderland town once supported roughly 70,000 people through the Porfiriato boom. Flooding, revolution and falling ore prices emptied it by the early 1900s; crumbling haciendas, smelter ruins and open shafts sit half-reclaimed by scrub, artists slowly resettling the centre.
s: Silver mining town abandoned to cactus and quiet
q: Mineral de Pozos San Luis de la Paz
_facts: Once-70,000-strong silver town now a near-empty adobe ruin

w: Quartz gold from the Blackwater Shaft supported over 600 residents through the 1930s, with a school, hospital and hall carved from West Coast bush. When the shaft flooded and collapsed in July 1951, the mine was abandoned outright and the town emptied within months, its foundations now walked by conservation trails.
s: Gold town abandoned within months of a shaft collapse
_facts: A whole town vanished within months of one shaft collapse

w: US Army engineers reshaped a rocky islet into a 350-foot concrete warship hull, armed with 14-inch naval guns, to guard the mouth of Manila Bay from 1914. Japanese troops held it through most of WWII until Americans pumped fuel into its vents and ignited it in 1945; the scorched hulk still sits offshore.
s: The concrete battleship guarding Manila Bay
q: Fort Drum (El Fraile Island) Cavite City
_facts: An entire island rebuilt into the shape of a battleship

w: Copper hauled from this pit for roughly a thousand years once supplied two-thirds of Europe's demand and bankrolled Sweden's 17th-century wars. A Midsummer's Eve collapse in 1687 gouged out the vast crater still visible today. Mining ended in 1992; tours now descend the old fire-set tunnels of this UNESCO site.
s: Thousand-year copper pit that funded an empire
_facts: The copper pit that financed Sweden's age as a great power

w: Eleven hotels, a brewery and the region's first public pool served 3,500 gold miners at this boomtown's 1907 peak, with four trains daily from Kalgoorlie. The Cosmopolitan mine's decline emptied it through the century; fewer than 20 remain, and the surviving Grand Hotel still pours drinks among ruined streets.
s: 3,500-strong gold town now down to one open pub
_facts: Once 3,500 strong, now a living ghost town with one pub left

w: Black volcanic tuff walls raised by Russian imperial engineers in the 1830s garrisoned troops guarding the Ottoman frontier above what was then Alexandropol. Later Soviet use gave way to abandonment; roofless barrack blocks and gun emplacements stand open to the wind beside the Mother Armenia statue.
s: Tsarist fortress abandoned above a border city
_facts: Tsarist border fortress standing empty over Armenia's edge

w: A herring-oil factory raised in 1934 became the largest concrete building in Iceland and Europe's first automated fish plant, its conveyor belts and cookers feeding a boom village of 260. The herring vanished by the late 1940s and the factory closed in 1954; caretakers now run a hotel beside its rusting machinery.
s: Iceland's largest concrete building, left to rust
_facts: Iceland's largest concrete building, now a rusting relic

w: A 1920s lakeside spa town of 1,500 residents drew 25,000 tourists a year for its supposedly healing waters, until a broken dike sent a ten-metre flood over it in 1985. Waters receded only after 2009, revealing a petrified, salt-white skeleton of hotels and trees, home to one former resident until his death in 2024.
s: Resort town that spent 25 years underwater
_facts: A resort town spent 25 years drowned, then resurfaced salt-white

w: The Glaoui clan built this High Atlas stronghold from 1860 with some 300 craftsmen laying zellij tile and carved cedar ceilings, wealth built on the caravan route and later collaboration with French rule. Independence in 1957 stripped the family's power; the palace's reception halls stand roofless above the village.
s: Warlord's palace abandoned after independence
_facts: A warlord's opulent palace stripped bare after independence

w: Greek colonists from Chalcis founded this settlement around 640 BC on a rock formation resembling a splayed hand, later fortified by Norman lords as a feudal seat. A violent 1783 earthquake and years of decline drove residents out by the 1960s; volunteers have since part-restored its stone lanes as a ghost village.
s: Five-fingered clifftop village emptied by earthquake
_facts: Ancient hand-shaped clifftop village, nearly lost to time

w: A once-decaying block of Callao's historic port district, anchored by the restored Casa Ronald building, now covered in more than sixty murals by local and international artists. Galleries, a rooftop and a cafe occupy the renovated interiors, a revival locals credit for pulling Callao out of Lima's tourist blind spot.
s: Faded port district reborn as an open-air gallery
_facts: Renovated port district reddit Lima threads cite as the real street-art hub

w: A pedestrian path descending through a garden-lined ravine in Barranco, crossed partway down by the Bridge of Sighs and shaded by ficus trees and bougainvillea. It runs from the district's colonial core down toward the Costa Verde clifftop, a quieter route to the ocean than the crowded boardwalk above.
s: Barranco's bougainvillea-lined ravine walk to the sea
_facts: Barranco locals' quieter alternative walk to the sea, off the main boardwalk

w: A small, actively bubbling mud volcano roughly fifty kilometres northeast of Cartagena, its crater reached by a wooden staircase and holding ten to fifteen bathers at once in warm grey mud. Visitors float rather than swim, dense enough that sinking is nearly impossible, then rinse off in a nearby lagoon.
s: A 15-metre mud volcano you climb and float in
_facts: Reddit Colombia threads rate it as Cartagena's weirdest worthwhile day trip

w: A freshwater sinkhole lagoon on the north coast near Cabrera, ringed by limestone cliffs and reachable by a rope swing, ladder or zipline into the water. Far from the Punta Cana resort strip, it stays mostly a local swimming hole, its interconnected caves popular with free divers rather than package tourists.
s: Freshwater sinkhole lagoon locals swim and dive in
_facts: Sinkhole lagoon reddit Dominican Republic threads flag over Punta Cana's resorts

w: A chain of turquoise limestone cenotes fed by underground rivers near Nenton, close enough to the Mexican border that some routes require hiking and swimming between pools. Reached only by rough roads through Guatemala's western highlands, it stays largely unvisited compared with the far more famous Semuc Champey.
s: Turquoise cenotes near the Mexican border
_facts: Remote cenote chain Guatemala travel threads flag as an unspoiled Semuc Champey alternative

w: Cacao beans get roasted, cracked and conched on site inside a 160-year-old merchant house at the mouth of Baba-dori, the old pilgrim approach into Izumo Taisha. Pilgrims duck in between shrine visits for a single-origin bar or drinking chocolate, a genuine bean-to-bar operation this far from Tokyo's chocolate scene.
s: Bean-to-bar chocolate steps from Izumo Taisha
_facts: Named among the best cafes to pair with an Izumo Taisha pilgrimage, a Shimane city few foreign visitors reach

w: Set inside the Matsue History Museum, this teahouse serves matcha and seasonal wagashi looking onto a karesansui garden that borrows the black keep of Matsue Castle as part of the scene. Sweets rotate with the almanac, quieter and cheaper than the cafes clustered outside the castle gate.
s: Matcha teahouse borrowing Matsue Castle's keep
_facts: Recommended repeatedly as the calmer alternative to Matsue's tourist-clogged castle-side cafes

w: Pouring siphon coffee since 1950 in Hiroshima's Ebisucho entertainment district, this kissaten still serves its egg sandwich under fluorescent light and vinyl booths untouched by renovation. It outlasted the postwar rebuild and the third-wave coffee boom alike, regulars on the same stools for decades.
s: 1950 siphon-coffee kissaten in Ebisucho
_facts: Named among Hiroshima's few genuine, unrenovated 1950s kissaten as retro cafe culture goes viral nationwide

w: Built by the Japanese merchant Hirotsu in the colonial period, this wooden mansion in Gunsan's Sinheung-dong keeps its tatami rooms and walled garden essentially intact, rare for a private house rather than a temple. Heritage-listed since 2005, its stillness now draws film crews and Seoul day-trippers.
s: Colonial-era merchant mansion frozen in the 1930s
_facts: Reddit's koreatravel regulars point to Gunsan's colonial quarter over Jeonju as the less-crowded pick

w: Trading since 1945, right after liberation, Leesungdang is Korea's oldest continuously operating bakery, still turning out its signature red-bean anpan from the same Gunsan shopfront that later spawned four Seoul branches. Locals queue past the newer outposts, insisting the dough tastes different at the original.
s: Korea's oldest working bakery, founded 1945
_facts: A near-mandatory local stop that keeps Gunsan on Korean and Reddit food-trip itineraries alike

w: Opened in 2023 on the site of the Guoshengpu outpost, a coastal defence post off-limits for decades, this cafe looks straight across the water to Cape Yehliu and the Dadu range. The restricted history is part of the draw: a deck now sits where soldiers once watched for landings, coffee replacing the checkpoint.
s: Cafe on a former restricted military outpost
_facts: A newly opened North Coast viewpoint cafe that's rapidly become the coast's most-shared new spot

a: Nanmen Road, opposite the Confucius Temple
w: A 38-centimetre gap between two buildings on Nanmen Road, opposite Tainan's Confucius Temple, is the only way in, squeezing through to a second-floor cafe of bold colour and high ceilings inside an old mansion. Running since the 1990s, it predates narrow-entrance cafes becoming an Instagram trope elsewhere.
s: Cafe reached through a 38cm-wide gap
_facts: One of Tainan's original hidden-entrance cafes, still cited as the backstreet benchmark near the temple

w: A disused cattle shed in Miaoquan village near Nanchang's Meiling forest park has been rebuilt into a book cafe where a barista's award-winning latte art draws over 200 visitors on weekends, most repeat customers. It fronts a wider wave of Jiangxi villages turning farm buildings into cafes and reading rooms.
s: A village cowshed reborn as a book cafe
q: Zai Fu Cowshed Book Cafe Nanchang
_facts: Profiled by state media as the leading example of China's rural cowshed-to-cafe revival trend

w: Down an easy-to-miss alley off Kotugodalla Street, near Kandy's train and bus stations, this cafe seats fewer than ten tables and keeps its menu to granola bowls and a handful of coffee drinks. It went viral on TikTok for the hard-to-find entrance, but the quiet, plant-lined courtyard keeps locals returning.
s: Fewer than ten tables down a Kandy alleyway
_facts: A Kandy institution that turned viral online while staying a genuine local hangout

w: At around 1,200 metres above the Uva tea country, this cliff-edge viewpoint drops away with the same sudden mist and sheer scale as the famous World's End at Horton Plains, minus the entry queue. Reaching it means a bus to Passara then the Pitamaruwa road into Madulsima, a route worked out from local hiking forums.
s: A misty cliff-edge viewpoint above Uva's tea hills
_facts: Increasingly shared as Sri Lanka's uncrowded answer to the overrun Horton Plains World's End

w: A half-hour bus ride northeast of central Pokhara, this hilltop at roughly 1,444 metres gives a panoramic sweep of the Annapurna and Dhaulagiri ranges with Phewa Lake below, and almost none of Sarangkot's sunrise crowds. Locals hike or drive up for the same view tourists queue for elsewhere in the valley.
s: Local sunrise hilltop over the Annapurnas, no crowds
_facts: Steadily gaining traction as Pokhara's quieter alternative to the overcrowded Sarangkot sunrise viewpoint

w: Three kilometres north of the Boudhanath stupa, this Tibetan Buddhist monastery houses more than 360 monks and runs meditation and philosophy courses open to travellers with no experience required. Its hillside setting above the valley smog makes it a favourite detour for travellers who find Boudhanath too crowded.
s: Hilltop monastery running walk-in meditation courses
_facts: A working monastery repeatedly flagged as calmer and more accessible than the stupa it sits above

w: Set in a Portuguese-era bungalow and garden in a quiet Calangute backstreet, this secondhand bookshop and cafe has become a fixture for readers who want something beyond Goa's beach shacks. Curated shelves lean toward Indian fiction, and the shaded courtyard doubles as a reading room away from the tourist strip.
s: A used-book haven in a century-old Goan bungalow
_facts: Consistently named among Goa's few genuine literary hideaways away from Calangute's party-beach scene

w: Ndalem Natan, a Javanese heritage house built around 1857 in the old silver-working quarter of Kotagede, now combines a bookstore, cafe, small museum and guesthouse under one roof. Original teak beams and courtyards stay intact around the coffee tables, a quieter alternative to Kotagede's silver-shop tourist trail.
s: Cafe, bookstore and museum inside an 1857 mansion
_facts: A heritage-house cafe-museum hybrid gaining traction as Kotagede's alternative to the silver-shop crowds

w: Reached through an alley behind a Dago hotel, this Japanese-inspired cafe of dark wood and low light became a local favourite for its quiet, tucked-away feel long before it showed up on travel apps. Bandung's Dago strip is thick with cafes; this one trades on being genuinely hard to stumble on.
s: Japanese-style cafe hidden behind a Dago hotel
_facts: Regularly singled out in Indonesian cafe guides as Dago's actual hidden gem, not just a marketing label

w: A working farm outside Tagaytay reworked into a Japanese-style ramen house and staycation resort, with wooden walkways strung between garden plots and ponds rather than a single dining room. It has spread fast on Filipino TikTok for the aesthetic rather than the ridge views tourists usually chase in Tagaytay proper.
s: Japanese-themed ramen farm-resort near Tagaytay
_facts: A Cavite farm-resort near Tagaytay going viral on Filipino social media well outside the usual ridge lookouts

w: Named rahsia, Malay for secret, this cafe sits up a quiet staircase in Ipoh's Taman Canning, feeling private enough that first-time visitors often double back to check the building. Its salted-caramel jingga latte and hushed upper-floor seating made it a favourite away from Ipoh's old-town coffee shops.
s: An upstairs Ipoh cafe named literally 'secret'
_facts: One of Ipoh's newer hidden-cafe wave, named for its own hard-to-find, secret-feeling entrance

w: Eleven roadside stone monuments run the seven kilometres between Roc and Hum, carved in 1977 to mark the region's Glagolitic script heritage. The alley ends at a single stone gate into a town of thirty residents, often called the smallest in the world, with cellars still stocked with mistletoe brandy.
s: Stone sculpture trail to the world's smallest town
_facts: Frequently named Istria's most underrated day trip on regional travel forums, bypassed for Motovun and Groznjan.

n: St Cyril and Methodius School Museum
w: Founded in 1837, this was one of the first Bulgarian-language schools operating under Ottoman rule, its wood-beamed classrooms preserved with era desks and re-enactor tableaux. Koprivshtitsa itself, two hours from Sofia, is a National Revival showcase of 383 protected houses that most itineraries skip entirely.
s: 1837 schoolhouse in a National Revival time capsule
q: St Cyril and Methodius School Museum Koprivshtitsa
_facts: Named repeatedly as Bulgaria's most overlooked historic town, overshadowed by Plovdiv and Veliko Tarnovo.

w: Tucked past the public toilets on the edge of this clifftop village above Grasse, an unmarked terrace opens onto a sheer drop and the whole Cote d'Azur coastline. Gourdon's main square draws day-trippers for the castle and gardens; almost none of them wander the extra fifty metres to find the actual panorama.
s: Unmarked clifftop terrace above Grasse
_facts: A recurring tip in regional travel threads as the view Gourdon's postcard shots never show.

w: Beneath a Dominican convent in this Umbrian hill town, an Inquisition tribunal room and adjoining cell sit exactly as rediscovered in 1979 by a group of local speleologists chasing rumours of a hidden chapel. The cell's walls carry desperate graffiti scratched by eighteenth-century prisoners awaiting trial.
s: Inquisition torture room found by cavers in 1979
q: Sala dei Tormenti, Narni Sotterranea Narni
_facts: A well-documented but still under-visited site, bypassed by the Rome-Assisi rail corridor most tourists follow.

n: MIAU - Museo Inacabado de Arte Urbano
w: A depopulating mountain village of roughly three hundred people invited street artists in 2014 to paint its facades, gates and walls rather than let houses stand empty; more than 160 murals by over a hundred artists now cover a town with no gallery walls, no doors and no admission fee, still gaining pieces.
s: Dying village turned wall-to-wall open gallery
q: MIAU - Museo Inacabado de Arte Urbano Fanzara
_facts: A minor cause celebre in street-art circles for reviving a nearly-abandoned village purely through murals, still under most Spain itineraries' radar.

w: A hermit-dug cave chapel is carved into a sandstone cliff on Dealul Plesu, origins disputed between medieval Orthodox monks and older, half-legendary cults; a hole cut through the rock ceiling lets a shaft of light onto the altar. Reachable only by forest track, it draws pilgrims and mystics rather than coach parties.
s: Cave chapel with a hole cut for a skylight
q: Sinca Veche rock hermitage Sinca Veche
_facts: A perennial 'weirdest place in Romania' pick in regional forums thanks to its disputed pre-Christian origins.

w: A brewpub was raised on the site of a thirteenth-century Franciscan monastery, its heated courtyard garden sitting over ground once used for monastic burials. Founded in 1998 as one of Ireland's first modern microbreweries, it still draws mostly Cork regulars rather than Dublin-bound coach parties.
s: Craft brewery on a Franciscan burial ground
_facts: Regularly cited as proof Cork's beer scene outclasses Dublin's without the crowds.

w: A wood-fired sauna raft is moored off Rindo island, thirty minutes from Stockholm by ferry, reachable by rowing a short stretch from the beach or hailing a water taxi. Locals book it for birthdays, alternating the hot room with jumps into the archipelago's cold water, largely unknown outside Vaxholm.
s: Floating wood-fired sauna in the archipelago
_facts: Described by locals as Stockholm's best-kept secret, absent from most archipelago itineraries centred on Vaxholm's fortress.

w: A medieval keep from Lier's old fortifications carries, since 1930, thirteen dials built by self-taught clockmaker Louis Zimmer, tracking the metonic cycle, the equation of time and the phases of the moon. Lier, a small town between Antwerp and Mechelen, rarely features on itineraries built around Bruges and Ghent.
s: Thirteen-dial astronomical clock on a medieval keep
_facts: A minor obsession among horology fans, entirely absent from mainstream Belgium trip planning.

w: Farmers from the surrounding Seeland fill this old town square several mornings a week with produce, bread, cheese and flowers, a ritual for a bilingual city most travellers skip between Bern and Neuchatel. Biel/Bienne's medieval core, arcaded and largely untouristed, surprises visitors expecting only industry.
s: Farmers' market in a bilingual city tourists skip
_facts: Repeatedly flagged as one of Switzerland's most overlooked old towns, hidden behind Biel's industrial and watchmaking reputation.

w: A wooden platform cantilevers thirty metres out from a mountainside above the Aurlandsfjord, glass-topped at the edge with no railing to break the drop. Six miles north of tourist-clogged Flam, Aurland gets a fraction of the cruise-ship footfall, so a platform rivalling any Norwegian fjord view stands nearly empty.
s: Railless glass-edged platform above the fjord
_facts: Regularly recommended as the fjord view worth taking over Flam's, without Flam's cruise-ship crowds.

w: Built by Fela Kuti's children as spiritual successor to his original Shrine club, the New Afrika Shrine in Ikeja keeps Afrobeat alive with free weekly sets from Femi and Seun Kuti before crowds that treat the open-air hall as sacred ground. Portraits and shrine-like decor tie it directly back to the genre's birthplace.
s: Rebuilt home of Fela Kuti's Afrobeat, still nightly
_facts: living heart of Afrobeat, direct successor to Fela Kuti's original club

w: Opened in 1933 in Yokohama's portside Noge district, Chigusa was bombed out in 1945, rebuilt its record collection through the occupation years, closed again in 2007, then was resurrected in 2012 by devoted regulars near its original spot. Vinyl still spins in the room that helped seed Japan's postwar jazz culture.
s: Japan's oldest jazz cafe, revived twice since 1933
_facts: Japan's oldest surviving jazz cafe, saved by community effort more than once

w: Owner Sugawara Seiji converted a family warehouse in provincial Ichinoseki into a jazz-listening room in 1970, naming it for Count Basie. The bandleader heard of the tribute and visited in 1980, arriving by wheelchair up ramps Sugawara built specially. Fans still travel far for its reputedly unrivaled acoustics.
s: Remote jazz kissa Count Basie himself once visited
_facts: obscure rural jazz kissa its namesake, Count Basie, actually visited in person

w: Started by a divorcing couple unsure what to do with the shared belongings of their relationship, this collection holds thousands of donated breakup objects, each with a short anonymous note on what it meant and why it ended. An axe used to chop up an ex's furniture sits under glass as a monument to heartbreak.
s: Breakup objects and the stories behind them
_facts: Crowdsourced museum of heartbreak that spawned a global franchise

w: Assistant attorney general Barry Levenson began collecting mustard jars in 1986 after the Red Sox blew the World Series, and the hobby grew into a roadside institution holding over 6,000 mustards from 70-plus countries. Free tastings run from a refrigerated case, and the gift shop sells mustard ice cream.
s: 6,000 jars of mustard, free tastings included
_facts: World's largest mustard collection, born from a bad baseball loss

w: Founded by lawnmower racer and restorer Brian Radam, this shop-front museum traces two centuries of grass-cutting technology, from Edwin Budding's 1830 patent to a mower once owned by Prince Charles. Vintage racing mowers and steam-powered cutters fill the cramped display, tribute to a very British obsession.
s: Two centuries of lawnmowers, including royal ones
_facts: Only museum in the world devoted purely to lawnmowers

w: Sanitation reformer Bindeshwar Pathak built this museum to make toilet history impossible to ignore, tracing 4,500 years of latrines from Harappan drainage systems to Louis XIV's velvet commode chair and a Victorian toilet disguised as a bookcase, underpinning Sulabh's public-toilet movement across India.
s: 4,500 years of toilets, from Harappa to Versailles
q: Sulabh International Museum of Toilets Delhi
_facts: Serious sanitation-history museum wrapped around a bathroom-humor collection

w: Potter Chez Galip began this collection in 1979 after a friend moved away, keeping a lock of her hair in his cave workshop; word spread and thousands of women visiting Avanos began leaving their own locks, each pinned with a name and address. More than 16,000 hair samples now cover the cave walls and ceiling.
s: 16,000 women's hair locks pinned to cave walls
_facts: Accidental collection that grew into a record-holding hair archive

w: Hormel Foods built this museum in its hometown to celebrate the canned meat it introduced in 1937 and shipped by the hundreds of millions of cans to feed Allied troops in WWII. Interactive exhibits include a canning-line race game and a wall of international flavor variants.
s: Canned-meat history, with a can-packing race game
_facts: Corporate hometown museum devoted to one specific canned meat

w: Gignese once supplied much of Europe with hand-made umbrellas, and this two-story museum, shaped like three overlapping umbrellas, preserves that trade with roughly 1,500 pieces spanning Napoleonic-era parasols to Belle Epoque folding umbrellas with carved ivory handles carried across the Alps by itinerant menders.
s: 1,500 umbrellas in a building shaped like three of them
_facts: Village-industry museum for a craft almost nobody else preserves

w: La Crosse calls itself the Barbed Wire Capital of the World, and this museum backs the claim with more than 2,000 distinct wire patterns patented from the 1870s onward, alongside the hand tools used to string fence across the Great Plains. Exhibits explain how barbed wire ended the open range and sparked range wars.
s: 2,000+ barbed wire patterns that fenced the prairie
q: Kansas Barbed Wire Museum La Crosse
_facts: Only accredited museum devoted purely to barbed wire

w: Former Suwon mayor Sim Jae-duck, nicknamed Mr. Toilet for his sanitation advocacy, had his own house built in the shape of a toilet bowl and willed it to the city as a museum on his death in 2009. Surrounding gardens display sculptures on toilet history, tied to Sim's founding of the World Toilet Association.
s: A house shaped like a toilet, built by 'Mr. Toilet'
_facts: Sanitation activist's own toilet-shaped home turned into a museum

w: A 19th-century tax on grave plots led Guanajuato's cemetery keepers to disinter unpaid graves, and the region's mineral-rich, arid soil had naturally mummified many of the bodies inside. Over a hundred are now displayed standing upright in glass cases, clothing and expressions frozen from the moment of exhumation.
s: 100+ naturally mummified bodies from unpaid graves
_facts: Accidental mummies created by burial-tax non-payment, now on display
